topics.title: Character of an induced module
objectives: Character of an induced module. Trace on coset blocks, off-diagonal contribution, representative independence, and the full-group average with the H factor.

passages.excerpt: Let R be a commutative unital ring, G finite, H a subgroup and V finite free over R with an R[H] action of character $\chi(h)=\operatorname{tr}\rho(h)$. The induced module is finite free by the coset-coordinate theorem. Choose T for left cosets, with inclusions $i_t:V\to U$ and projections $p_t:U\to V$.
\chi_{\mathrm{Ind}V}(g)=\sum_{t\in T:\ t^{-1}gt\in H}\chi(t^{-1}gt).
|H|\in R^\times\Longrightarrow\chi_{\mathrm{Ind}V}(g)=\frac1{|H|}\sum_{a\in G:\ a^{-1}ga\in H}\chi(a^{-1}ga).
In a basis grouped by the coset copies, the diagonal matrix block of $L_g$ at t is $p_tL_gi_t$. The trace of the full matrix is the sum of traces of these diagonal blocks.

If $gt=t^{\prime}h$ with $t^{\prime}\ne t$, the output of $L_gi_t$ lies in the other copy. Therefore $p_tL_gi_t=0$. This says its diagonal block is zero, even though the original operator is invertible and has not killed the vectors.
If $gt=th$, then $h=t^{-1}gt\in H$, and $p_tL_gi_t(v)=hv$. Its trace is $\chi(t^{-1}gt)$. Summing proves the fixed-coset formula without division by a group order.

Replace t by $th_0$. The fixed-coset condition is unchanged, and the element in H becomes $h_0^{-1}(t^{-1}gt)h_0$. Its matrix is conjugated by $\rho(h_0)$. Over a commutative ring $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ by a double-index sum, so trace is unchanged. This proves representative independence.

Every $a\in G$ has one form $a=th$ with $h\in H$. Then $a^{-1}ga=h^{-1}(t^{-1}gt)h$. Membership in H is equivalent to the fixed-coset condition, and all |H| values within a qualifying coset have the same trace. Thus the full-group sum is |H| times the fixed-coset sum.
Divide only if $|H|1_R$ is a unit. The full-group averaged formula follows. At g=1 the fixed-coset sum is $[G:H]\operatorname{rank}_R V$. If no conjugate of g lies in H, its character value is zero.
At identity all three blocks are fixed, giving trace three. At a transposition exactly one coset is fixed and its correction has sign minus one, giving trace minus one.
With coset basis $1\otimes1,r\otimes1$, r has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, so its trace is zero.

On D8 classes $1,r^2,\{r,r^3\},\{s,r^2s\},\{rs,r^3s\}$, traces are $(2,-2,0,0,0)$. The class sizes are $(1,1,2,2,2)$, so the weighted norm is $(4+4)/8=1$, independently confirming the constructed irreducible.

The induced-character formula gives the same values. At rotation $r^k$, both cosets are fixed and the trace is $i^k+i^{-k}$. At a reflection, the two cosets are exchanged and there is no diagonal block.
Over R=F2 with H=G=C2 and V trivial of rank one, the fixed-coset formula gives trace one. The averaged formula would divide by $|H|=0$ in R and is undefined. The coset formula survives this boundary.

topics.title: Extend induction to class functions
objectives: Extend induction to class functions, class indicators, H-class fusion, and centralizer-ratio value formulas.

passages.excerpt: (\operatorname{Ind}f)(g)=\sum_j\frac{|C_G(g)|}{|C_H(h_j)|}f(h_j).
\operatorname{Ind}(1_K)=\frac{|C_G(h)|}{|C_H(h)|}\,1_{h^G}\quad(K=h^H).

Extending f by zero off H is usually not G-conjugacy-invariant. Average all of its G-conjugates instead. Substituting $x\mapsto yx$ shows the resulting function has the same value at $g$ and $y^{-1}gy$, so induction maps class functions to class functions and is linear.

For a fixed target $h\in g^G\cap H$, the set of x with $x^{-1}gx=h$ has size $|C_G(g)|$. If x0 is one such conjugator, every other is uniquely $c x_0$ with $c\in C_G(g)$, as direct substitution verifies.

Therefore the averaged sum equals $|C_G(g)|/|H|$ times $\sum_{h\in g^G\cap H}f(h)$. Group by H classes. Each class of h_j has size $|H|/|C_H(h_j)|$ and f is constant there, giving the centralizer-ratio formula.

For the H-class indicator $1_K$, only one term survives on its fused G class, with the stated ratio, and every other G class has value zero. Since class indicators form a basis, this also derives the formula for all class functions.

In the D8 subgroup of S4 fixed in the preceding matrix lesson, class fusion yields $(\operatorname{Ind}f)(1)=3f(1)$, $(\operatorname{Ind}f)(2)=f(s)$, $(\operatorname{Ind}f)(2^2)=f(r^2)+2f(rs)$, $(\operatorname{Ind}f)(3)=0$, and $(\operatorname{Ind}f)(4)=f(r)$.

The coefficients come from centralizers: for a double transposition, $|C_{S_4}|=8$, while the D8 centralizer orders are eight for r squared and four for rs. The two H classes therefore contribute weights one and two. This is class fusion, not double-coset module decomposition.
It is a class function but not a nonzero actual character, because its identity value is zero while some other value is not.

In S3 a chosen transposition subgroup contains one transposition but not its two conjugates. Extension by zero gives different values on the same S3 conjugacy class, so it is not yet a class function on G.

objectives: Restriction/induction multiplicity matrices, S5/A4 row-column reciprocity, and D8-to-S4 numerical induction.

passages.excerpt: In S5 row order $1,\varepsilon,v,\varepsilon v,w,\varepsilon w,x$, restriction gives rows $(1,1,1,1)$ twice, $(4,0,1,1)$ twice, $(5,1,-1,-1)$ twice and $(6,-2,0,0)$ once.

For any restricted row $(d,b,c,c)$, the multiplicities are $(d+3b+8c)/12$ for $1$, $(d+3b-4c)/12$ for each of $\lambda,\lambda^2$, and $(d-b)/4$ for $\tau$. The latter follows from $\overline\tau=(3,-1,0,0)$ and H class weights.
Substituting each of the seven rows gives the displayed matrix. For example $(5,1,-1,-1)$ yields $(0,1,1,1)$, and $(6,-2,0,0)$ yields $(0,0,0,2)$.

Frobenius reciprocity identifies the same integer as the multiplicity of $\chi$ in $\operatorname{Ind}_{A_4}^{S_5}\psi$. Thus the columns, without another class-value computation, are the complete induction decompositions in the reading.

The index is ten. Each column has weighted degree ten times its H degree, checking both the class map and matrix orientation. Rows encode restriction; columns encode induction. Reversing this interpretation swaps the source and target dimensions.
$\operatorname{Ind}1=1+\varepsilon+v+\varepsilon v$.
$\operatorname{Ind}\lambda=\operatorname{Ind}\lambda^2=w+\varepsilon w$.
$\operatorname{Ind}\tau=v+\varepsilon v+w+\varepsilon w+2x$.
Its inner product with $\tau$ is $(6\cdot3+3(-2)(-1))/12=2$.
This H has order twelve and fixes the fifth letter. Its index in S5 is ten. Treating it as A5 would use order sixty, erase the two A4 three-cycle classes and produce the wrong matrix.

The permutations $r^i$ and $r^is$, $0\le i<4$, are distinct, and the relation moves s past powers of r, proving they form the eight-element dihedral subgroup. Conjugation yields the five classes listed in the objects paragraph.

Taking weighted inner products with the D8 rows gives the displayed decompositions. For example the standard row pairs with u to give $(3\cdot2+(-1)(-2))/8=1$, and with $\lambda_{-+}$ to give $(3-1+2+2+2)/8=1$.

The matrix rows are ordered $1,\varepsilon,v,\varepsilon v,q$ and columns $\lambda_{++},\lambda_{+-},\lambda_{-+},\lambda_{--},u$. Reading its columns by reciprocity gives $\operatorname{Ind}\lambda_{++}=1+q$, $\operatorname{Ind}\lambda_{+-}=\varepsilon v$, $\operatorname{Ind}\lambda_{-+}=v$, $\operatorname{Ind}\lambda_{--}=\varepsilon+q$, and $\operatorname{Ind}u=v+\varepsilon v$.

All induced degrees are three times the source degree because the index is three. The two middle linear characters induce irreducibly, while the trivial and sign-compatible linear characters induce reducibly. Equal subgroup degrees do not imply the same induction behavior.
Its values are $(3,1,-1,0,-1)$ on the S4 class order $1,2,2^2,3,4$, not simply the D8 values extended by zero.

The s-class here consists of transpositions, while the rs-class consists of double transpositions. Swapping those two classes changes which linear character induces to v. Specify the actual embedding before naming the rows.
\operatorname{Ind}1=1+\varepsilon+v+\varepsilon v,\qquad\operatorname{Ind}\lambda=\operatorname{Ind}\overline\lambda=v+\varepsilon v+q.
Any restricted S4 row has form $(d,a,a)$ on $1,c,c^2$. Its trivial multiplicity is $(d+2a)/3$. Its lambda and conjugate-lambda multiplicities both equal $(d-a)/3$, since $\omega+\omega^2=-1$.

The S4 degree-three rows have a=0, so each restricts to $1+\lambda+\overline\lambda$. The degree-two row has $(d,a)=(2,-1)$ and restricts to $\lambda+\overline\lambda$. Trivial and sign restrict to the trivial row. This gives every matrix entry.

Over C, the Hom adjunction makes the multiplicity of a G irreducible in an induced H module equal to its H multiplicity on restriction. Therefore reading each column proves the two induction formulas.

Independently use class fusion. The identity value is eight. Only the S4 three-cycle class intersects H nontrivially. Its centralizer has order three, as does H. Thus the induced value there is $\theta(c)+\theta(c^2)$, and it is zero on every other nonidentity S4 class.

This gives rows $(8,0,0,2,0)$ for the induced trivial character and $(8,0,0,-1,0)$ for either induced nontrivial character, in S4 class order $1,2,2^2,3,4$. Summing the listed irreducible rows recovers these values.
Its trivial multiplicity is $(2-2)/3=0$, and each nontrivial multiplicity is $(2+1)/3=1$.

Restriction has five G rows and three H columns. Induction uses those same coefficients with source and target roles reversed. A bare matrix transpose without row and column labels can attach a correct integer to the wrong representation.

topics.title: Order-21 group
objectives: Order-21 group. Quotient linear characters, conjugacy classes, two induced degree-three rows, period sums, and completeness.

passages.excerpt: Let G act on $\mathbb F_7$ by affine maps $x\mapsto2^jx+i$, with $i\in\mathbb F_7$ and $j\in\mathbb Z/3$. Write $a(x)=x+1$ and $b(x)=2x$. Then $a^7=b^3=1$ and $bab^{-1}=a^2$. Its normal subgroup H generated by a has order seven and index three. Put $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/7}$ and $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$.
u=\zeta+\zeta^2+\zeta^4=\tfrac{-1+i\sqrt7}{2},\quad v=\zeta^3+\zeta^5+\zeta^6=\overline u.
\operatorname{Irr}(G)=\{1,\mu,\mu^2,\chi,\overline\chi\},\quad\text{degrees }1,1,1,3,3.

There are exactly 21 distinct affine maps, so the presentation describes a concrete group. Conjugation by b partitions the six nonidentity a powers into exponent orbits $R=\{1,2,4\}$ and $N=\{3,5,6\}$. These give two classes of size three.

Conjugation by a permutes all seven elements of Hb, since multiplication by $1-2$ is invertible in F7. Similarly all Hb squared form one class of size seven. Quotient images distinguish these two classes. Thus class order $1,a^R,a^N,Hb,Hb^2$ has sizes $(1,3,3,7,7)$.

The quotient G/H of order three gives $\mu(a)=1$, $\mu(b)=\omega$ and its square. For the H character $\lambda(a)=\zeta$, induction has degree three. Normality and the coset trace formula give $\chi(a^k)=\zeta^k+\zeta^{2k}+\zeta^{4k}$ and zero off H.
For k in R this period is u; for k in N it is v. Since $1+\sum_{k=1}^6\zeta^k=0$, $u+v=-1$. Expanding uv gives three terms equal to one and each of $\zeta,\ldots,\zeta^6$ once, so $uv=3-1=2$.

Negation swaps R and N, so $v=\overline u$. Therefore u and v are roots of $z^2+z+2=0$. The imaginary part of u is positive: it equals $\sin(2\pi/7)+\sin(3\pi/7)-\sin(\pi/7)>0$. This selects the stated sign of the square root.

The induced character is actual and has norm $(9+3|u|^2+3|v|^2)/21=(9+6+6)/21=1$, hence is irreducible. Inducing $\lambda^3$ gives the distinct conjugate row. Their cross inner product is $(9+3(u^2+v^2))/21=0$, since $u^2+v^2=-3$.

The three linear rows and two degree-three rows have squared degrees $3+9+9=21$. Thus they form the complete table. The two b-class columns have zero in the degree-three rows because no conjugate of those elements lies in H.
Columns are $1,a^R,a^N,Hb,Hb^2$, with sizes $(1,3,3,7,7)$.
$\mu=(1,1,1,\omega,\omega^2)$.
$\overline\chi=(3,v,u,0,0)$.
Their induced values sum the same exponent orbit R, so they all give the same G row $\chi$.
At b no coset of H is fixed, since b is outside the normal subgroup H, so the trace is zero.

The exponent sets R and N are exchanged by negation, so the periods are complex conjugates, not individually real. Their discriminant is minus seven. Replacing them by real roots would contradict the norm and conjugation identities.

objectives: Induction product identity with a restricted character, induced degree, and the squared-multiplicity bound for an induced irreducible.

passages.excerpt: \operatorname{Ind}_H^G(\theta\,\operatorname{Res}_H^G\chi)=(\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\theta)\chi,\qquad\deg\operatorname{Ind}\theta=[G:H]\theta(1).
\sum_i n_i^2=\|\operatorname{Ind}\theta\|_G^2\le[G:H].

In the averaged induction sum at g, each qualifying $x^{-1}gx$ has $\chi(x^{-1}gx)=\chi(g)$ because chi is a G class function. Factor that common value out. The remaining sum is exactly $\operatorname{Ind}\theta(g)$, proving the character product identity in every column.

The corresponding module isomorphism sends $t\otimes(v\otimes w)$ to $(t\otimes v)\otimes tw$ for group elements $t\in G$, extended additively and complex-linearly. For balancing by $h\in H$, the left side with th maps to $(t\otimes hv)\otimes thw$, agreeing with the right side using $h(v\otimes w)=hv\otimes hw$. Thus it descends.

Its inverse sends $(t\otimes v)\otimes w$ to $t\otimes(v\otimes t^{-1}w)$. Replacing $(th,v)$ by $(t,hv)$ gives the same balanced tensor after applying the diagonal h action. Direct substitution gives both inverse identities, and multiplying t by any g shows equivariance. This proves the identity at the module level too.
At identity every coset is fixed. Each contributes $\dim V=\theta(1)$, yielding the degree formula. This holds for reducible V as well.

For the norm bound choose a transversal T of size m. Define $f_t(g)=\theta(t^{-1}gt)$ when the conjugate lies in H, and zero otherwise. The induced value is $\sum_t f_t(g)$. Cauchy-Schwarz gives $|\sum_t f_t(g)|^2\le m\sum_t|f_t(g)|^2$.

For each t, conjugation is a bijection from $tHt^{-1}$ to H, so $\sum_g|f_t(g)|^2=\sum_h|\theta(h)|^2=|H|$. Sum the inequality over G and divide by $|G|=m|H|$. The result is $\|\operatorname{Ind}\theta\|^2\le m$. Orthogonality identifies that norm with $\sum_i n_i^2$.

For an arbitrary H class function f the same proof gives $\|\operatorname{Ind}f\|_G^2\le m\|f\|_H^2$. The bare bound m therefore requires norm-one input, in particular an irreducible source character.
The right side is $(1+v)v=v+v^2=1+\varepsilon+2v$, giving the same six-dimensional module.
Its norm is $1^2+1^2=2$, which is less than the index three.
For H trivial and G=C3, inducing its unique irreducible gives the regular character, with three distinct linear summands and norm three, attaining the index bound.

If theta is twice the trivial character of H, its squared norm is four. Inducing multiplies every induced multiplicity by two, so the squared norm scales by four as well. The bound by the subgroup index alone no longer follows.

topics.title: Index-two induction classification for an irreducible subgroup character and its conjugate
objectives: Index-two induction classification for an irreducible subgroup character and its conjugate.

passages.excerpt: Let H be an index-two subgroup of finite G, choose $t\in G\setminus H$, and use complex characters. Let $\theta\in\operatorname{Irr}(H)$ have degree d and define $({}^t\theta)(h)=\theta(t^{-1}ht)$. H is normal, so this is another H irreducible. Let epsilon be the quotient sign character of G.
\operatorname{Res}_H^G\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\theta=\theta+{}^t\theta,\qquad \|\operatorname{Ind}\theta\|_G^2=1+\langle\theta,{}^t\theta\rangle_H.
{}^t\theta\ne\theta\Rightarrow\operatorname{Ind}\theta\text{ irreducible};\quad{}^t\theta=\theta\Rightarrow\operatorname{Ind}\theta=\chi+\varepsilon\chi,\ \chi|_H=\theta.

Choose transversal $1,t$. Because H is normal, each coset copy is H-invariant. On the first copy its action is theta, and on the second it is $h\mapsto\theta(t^{-1}ht)$. This proves the restriction identity.

Frobenius reciprocity gives the norm of the induced character as $\langle\theta,\theta+{}^t\theta\rangle_H$, equal to one or two. The induced module is actual, so norm one means irreducible and norm two means two distinct irreducibles once each.

If the two H characters differ, the induction is irreducible of degree $2d$. No G extension of theta can exist: conjugation by a G operator would identify theta with its outside conjugate. The induced character vanishes off H and is its own sign twist.

If the H characters agree, write $\operatorname{Ind}\theta=\chi_1+\chi_2$. Reciprocity gives multiplicity one of theta in each restriction. Hence each degree is at least d, while their sum is $2d$. Both degrees are therefore d and both restrictions are exactly theta.

By the index-two restriction pair classification, these two extensions are precisely $\chi$ and $\varepsilon\chi$. They are distinct and exhaust all irreducible G extensions of theta. This proves existence of extensions as well as the decomposition.

For a direct matrix construction in the invariant case, choose an invertible intertwiner T with $T\sigma(h)T^{-1}=\sigma(tht^{-1})$. Then $T^2\sigma(t^2)^{-1}$ commutes with every H operator, so Schur makes it a nonzero scalar c. Also T commutes with $\sigma(t^2)$. Rescale T by a square root of $c^{-1}$ to get $T^2=\sigma(t^2)$.

Assign the H action sigma and the outside representative action T. The conjugation rule and square rule verify the group law on $H\cup tH$. Choosing minus T gives the other extension. Availability of complex square roots is one reason this conclusion is stated over C.
The trivial theta is invariant, so its two extensions are the trivial and sign S3 rows; its induction is their sum.
For $\theta(r)=-1$, the conjugate is equal. The two degree-one extensions send r to minus one and the reflection to plus one or minus one; their sum is the induced row.

For G=C4, H generated by r squared and its real sign module, induction has r matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and is irreducible over R. Over C it splits into the i and minus-i linear characters. The complex index-two extension conclusion does not carry unchanged to R.

passages.excerpt: U\text{ irreducible}\iff\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb CG}(U)=1\qquad(0<\dim_{\mathbb C}U<\infty)

Let $G$ be finite and $U\ne0$ a finite-dimensional complex left $G$-module. Its commutant is the complex vector space $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb CG}(U)$ of linear maps $T$ with $T\rho(g)=\rho(g)T$ for every $g$.
Suppose $U$ is irreducible and $T\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb CG}(U)$. Since $U$ is nonzero and finite-dimensional over $\mathbb C$, $T$ has an eigenvalue $\lambda$.
Conversely, suppose $W$ is a nonzero proper submodule. Choose an ordinary vector-space projection $p:U\to W$ with $p|_W=I_W$.
The projection $P$ is neither zero nor the identity. A scalar idempotent over a field is zero or the identity, so $P$ is nonscalar.

The more general complex semisimple calculation is $U\cong\bigoplus_i S_i^{\oplus m_i}$ with pairwise nonisomorphic irreducibles. A map between distinct $S_i$ vanishes by Schur, while maps among $m_i$ equivalent copies form $M_{m_i}(\mathbb C)$.
Over $\mathbb R$, let $C_4$ act on $\mathbb R^2$ by $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. There is no real invariant line because $J$ has no real eigenvalue.
In characteristic three, let $S_3$ act on $\mathbb F_3^2$ by $r=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $s=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. The relations $r^3=s^2=I$ and $srs=r^{-1}$ hold.
The four scalar parameters give $\dim\operatorname{End}_G(U)=4$. Projection onto the first copy is a nonscalar idempotent.
Every equivariant map has diagonal form $\operatorname{diag}(a,b)$. The commutant has dimension two, equal to $1^2+1^2$, and the two coordinate projections exhibit the direct sum.
The zero module has an endomorphism space of dimension zero. It is excluded from irreducibility by definition.
\operatorname{Ind}_H^G V\text{ irreducible}\iff V\text{ irreducible and }{}^gV\not\cong V\text{ for all }g\in G\setminus H
Let $G$ be finite, $H\trianglelefteq G$, and $0<\dim_{\mathbb C}V<\infty$ with $H$-action $\sigma$. Put $U=\mathbb CG\otimes_{\mathbb CH}V$.
For $h\in H$, normality gives $ht=t(t^{-1}ht)$ with $t^{-1}ht\in H$. Hence $h(t\otimes v)=t\otimes\sigma(t^{-1}ht)v$.

Induction-restriction adjunction sends $F\in\operatorname{End}_G(U)$ to $v\mapsto F(1\otimes v)$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_H(V,\operatorname{Res}U)$. Its inverse sends an $H$-map $f$ to $b\otimes v\mapsto bf(v)$.
Assume first that $U$ is irreducible. The complex endomorphism criterion makes the total dimension one.

Conversely, suppose $V$ is irreducible and every nonidentity representative gives a nonisomorphic conjugate. All ${}^tV$ are irreducible, so Schur gives $\dim\operatorname{End}_H(V)=1$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_H(V,{}^tV)=0$ for $t\ne1$.

To replace representatives by all elements outside $H$, let $g^{\prime}=gh_0$ with $h_0\in H$. The invertible map $A=\sigma(h_0^{-1})$ satisfies $A\sigma(g^{-1}hg)=\sigma(g^{\prime-1}hg^{\prime})A$ for every $h\in H$.
Normality and complex semisimplicity have distinct jobs. Without normality, conjugation need not preserve $H$ and Mackey intersections replace full conjugates.

In the basis $1\otimes1,s\otimes1$, $r$ acts by $\operatorname{diag}(\zeta,\zeta^{-1})$ and $s$ swaps the two coordinates. The two distinct $r$-eigenlines are exchanged by $s$, which also gives a direct irreducibility check.

The induced module is the permutation representation on the two cosets. The sum of the coordinate vectors is trivial and their difference is sign, so $\operatorname{Ind}_{A_3}^{S_3}1\cong1\oplus\operatorname{sgn}$.
Let $G=C_4=\langle r\rangle$, $H=\langle r^2\rangle$ and let $r^2$ act on $V=\mathbb R$ by $-1$. All conjugates equal $V$ because $G$ is abelian.

passages.excerpt: x^{S_n}\text{ splits into two }A_n\text{-classes}\iff C_{S_n}(x)\subseteq A_n
Let $n\ge2$, $G=S_n$, $N=A_n$ and $x\in A_n$. The conjugacy class $x^G=\{gxg^{-1}:g\in G\}$ lies inside $A_n$, since sign is unchanged by conjugation.
Fix an odd $\tau\in S_n$. Every permutation lies in $A_n$ or $\tau A_n$.
If an odd $c$ centralizes $x$, every odd conjugator $g$ can be replaced by the even $gc^{-1}$. Indeed $(gc^{-1})x(gc^{-1})^{-1}=gxg^{-1}$.
Conversely, if $\tau x\tau^{-1}=axa^{-1}$ for some even $a$, then $a^{-1}\tau$ centralizes $x$ and is odd. Hence equality of the two possible classes forces an odd centralizer element.
The map $y\mapsto\tau y\tau^{-1}$ is a bijection between the two classes, so their sizes are equal. The orbit-stabilizer calculation makes the size precise.
This argument works for any index-two normal subgroup $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $x\in N$. The test is $C_G(x)\subseteq N$.
The inverse $(132)$ is obtained by the odd conjugator $(23)$. Every other conjugator differs from it by an even centralizer element, so no even conjugator sends $(123)$ to $(132)$.
Conjugation by $(45)$ sends $x$ to $(12354)$. This conjugator is odd and cannot be repaired, because the centralizer has no odd element.
For $x=(123)\in A_5$, the transposition $(45)$ centralizes $x$ because it moves only fixed points. Any odd conjugator can be repaired by $(45)$.

passages.excerpt: x^{S_n}\text{ splits in }A_n\iff \ell_1,\ldots,\ell_r\text{ are distinct odd integers}
Let $x\in A_n$ with $n\ge2$. Write its disjoint cycles on all $n$ letters, including every fixed point.

If $x$ has a disjoint cycle $c$ of even length, $c$ commutes with every other disjoint cycle and hence with $x$. Since $\operatorname{sgn}(c)=(-1)^{|c|-1}=-1$, the centralizer contains an odd element.

If two disjoint cycles of the same odd length are $c=(a_0\ldots a_{\ell-1})$ and $d=(b_0\ldots b_{\ell-1})$, define $s=\prod_{j=0}^{\ell-1}(a_jb_j)$. Conjugation by $s$ interchanges $c$ and $d$ and fixes the other cycles, so $sxs^{-1}=x$.
Conversely, suppose the full cycle lengths are distinct and odd. A permutation $z$ commuting with $x$ satisfies $z(x^j a)=x^jz(a)$.
On a cycle $c$ of length $\ell$, the choice $z(a)=c^t(a)$ forces $z(c^ja)=c^{j+t}(a)$ at every point. Thus the restriction of $z$ to that support is $c^t$.
This proof also computes $|C_{S_n}(x)|=\prod_i\ell_i$ in the distinct-length case. The split classes then have size $n!/(2\prod_i\ell_i)$.
In $A_7$, $(67)$ is an odd centralizer for the same written 5-cycle. The type $(5,1,1)$ has centralizer order $5\cdot2=10$ in $S_7$, and its 504 elements form one $A_7$-class.
For $y=(1234567)\in A_7$, the only cycle length is seven. The centralizer has order seven and is even.
Writing only $(123)$ for an element of $A_5$ hides the type $(3,1,1)$. The omitted fixed points give an odd centralizer $(45)$.

passages.excerpt: \exists!\,A^*\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb F}(Y,X),\qquad[A^*]_{\mathrm{ON}}=[A]_{\mathrm{ON}}^\dagger

Let $X,Y$ be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and $A:X\to Y$ linear. We use $\langle\alpha x,y\rangle=\alpha\langle x,y\rangle$ and $\langle x,\alpha y\rangle=\overline\alpha\langle x,y\rangle$.
For an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ of $X$, define $B(y)=\sum_i\langle y,Ae_i\rangle_Y e_i$. Each coefficient is linear in $y$, so $B:Y\to X$ is linear.
Write $x=\sum_i x_ie_i$. Then $\langle x,B(y)\rangle_X=\sum_i x_i\overline{\langle y,Ae_i\rangle_Y}=\sum_i x_i\langle Ae_i,y\rangle_Y=\langle Ax,y\rangle_Y$.
If $B$ and $C$ both satisfy the defining identity, $\langle x,(B-C)y\rangle=0$ for all $x,y$. Taking $x=(B-C)y$ gives $\|(B-C)y\|^2=0$, so $(B-C)y=0$ for every $y$.

For any bases, not necessarily orthonormal, the identity on every basis pair extends to all vectors. Indeed, if $x=\sum_i\alpha_i e_i$ and $y=\sum_j\beta_j f_j$, then $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\overline{\beta_j}\langle Ae_i,f_j\rangle$.
For orthonormal bases, $[A]_{ji}=\langle Ae_i,f_j\rangle$. The $(i,j)$ entry of $[A^*]$ is $\langle A^*f_j,e_i\rangle=\langle f_j,Ae_i\rangle=\overline{[A]_{ji}}$.
Uniqueness also proves $(BA)^*=A^*B^*$, $(A^*)^*=A$, and $(\lambda A)^*=\overline\lambda A^*$. For example, $\langle BAx,z\rangle=\langle Ax,B^*z\rangle=\langle x,A^*B^*z\rangle$.
The adjoint has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-i\end{pmatrix}$, so $A^*y=(2y,-iy)$. Directly, $\langle x,A^*y\rangle=2x_1\overline y+ix_2\overline y=\langle Ax,y\rangle$.
Uniqueness gives $P^*=P$. In an orthonormal basis its matrix is the symmetric matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$.
For $A:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$, $Az=iz$, ordinary transpose leaves the matrix $i$ unchanged. But $\langle ix,y\rangle=ix\overline y$ and $\langle x,iy\rangle=-ix\overline y$.

passages.excerpt: [A^*]_{f\to e}=G_X^{-1}[A]_{e\to f}^{\dagger}G_Y
Let $e=(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ and $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$ be arbitrary bases of inner-product spaces $X,Y$. The coordinate maps are $E:\mathbb F^n\to X$, $Ea=\sum_i a_ie_i$, and $F:\mathbb F^m\to Y$.
Expand $\langle Ea,Eb\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_j\overline{b_i}\langle e_j,e_i\rangle=b^\dagger G_Xa$. Conjugate symmetry gives $G_X^\dagger=G_X$.
For $A:X\to Y$, its coordinate matrix is $M=F^{-1}AE$. For the adjoint the domain and codomain reverse, so $N=E^{-1}A^*F$.
The equality holds for all $a$ and $b$. Testing standard coordinate basis columns proves $G_YM=N^\dagger G_X$.
Conversely, define $N=G_X^{-1}M^\dagger G_Y$ and the linear map $B=ENF^{-1}:Y\to X$. Substitution in the two coordinate pairings proves $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,By\rangle$ for every $x,y$.

Thus $[P^*]=M$ and $P^*=P$, while $M^T\ne M$. Self-adjointness is a property of the operator and inner product, not ordinary matrix symmetry in every basis.
The Gram matrices are $G_X=4$ and $G_Y=9$. The formula gives $N=(1/4)(4/3)9=3$.

passages.excerpt: \langle\operatorname{Ind}_H^G f,F\rangle_G=\langle f,\operatorname{Res}_H^G F\rangle_H,\qquad\operatorname{Ind}^*=\operatorname{Res}

For a finite group $G$, let $\mathrm{CF}(G)$ be the complex vector space of functions constant on conjugacy classes. Use the linear-first inner product $\langle f,F\rangle_G=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}f(g)\overline{F(g)}$.
Restriction of a $G$-class function is an $H$-class function because $H$-conjugacy is a special case of $G$-conjugacy. Induction is a class function on $G$.
The weighted form is Hermitian and positive definite. Indeed $\langle f,f\rangle_G=|G|^{-1}\sum_g|f(g)|^2$, which vanishes only for the zero function.

Expand $\langle\operatorname{Ind}f,F\rangle_G=(|G||H|)^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}\sum_{x:\,x^{-1}gx\in H}f(x^{-1}gx)\overline{F(g)}$. The change of variables $h=x^{-1}gx$ is a bijection between the summation pairs $(g,x)$ and $(h,x)\in H\times G$, with inverse $g=xhx^{-1}$.

Since $F$ is a class function, $F(xhx^{-1})=F(h)$. Therefore the sum becomes $(|G||H|)^{-1}\sum_{x\in G}\sum_{h\in H}f(h)\overline{F(h)}=|H|^{-1}\sum_{h\in H}f(h)\overline{F(h)}=\langle f,\operatorname{Res}F\rangle_H$.
Uniqueness follows directly too. If $B$ also satisfies the identity, then $\langle f,(B-\operatorname{Res})F\rangle_H=0$ for all $f,F$.
For a class $C$, the indicator $\delta_C$ equals one on $C$ and zero elsewhere. Distinct indicators are orthogonal, and their squared norms are $|C|/|G|$.
Induction sends $(a,b)$ to $(3a,b,0)$. In particular the nontrivial $H$ character $(1,-1)$ induces the character $(3,-1,0)$.
The algebra basis symbols $g\in G$ and the class-function coordinate indicators are different bases of different spaces. The character calculation connects them without identifying them.
For the raw coordinate restriction matrix $R$, its ordinary transpose sends $(a,b)$ to $(a,b,0)$. True induction sends it to $(3a,b,0)$.

passages.excerpt: \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Set}}(X\times A,Y)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Set}}(X,Y^A)

A category has objects, sets $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,Y)$ of morphisms with source and target, identity morphisms, and associative composition. In $R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ the objects are unital left $R$-modules and morphisms are $R$-linear maps.

Composition of $R$-linear maps is $R$-linear, identity maps are $R$-linear, and ordinary function composition is associative. Thus unital left modules and their linear maps form the category $R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$.
For a fixed set $A$, define $F(\alpha):X^{\prime}\times A\to X\times A$ by $(x^{\prime},a)\mapsto(\alpha(x^{\prime}),a)$. Define $U(\beta):Y^A\to Y^{\prime A}$ by $f\mapsto\beta\circ f$.
For $h:X\times A\to Y$, define $\widehat h:X\to Y^A$ by $\widehat h(x)(a)=h(x,a)$. For $f:X\to Y^A$, define $\check f:X\times A\to Y$ by $\check f(x,a)=f(x)(a)$.

For $\alpha:X^{\prime}\to X$ and $\beta:Y\to Y^{\prime}$, both currying routes evaluate at $(x^{\prime},a)$ to $\beta(h(\alpha(x^{\prime}),a))$. Hence $\widehat{\beta\circ h\circ(\alpha\times1_A)}=U(\beta)\circ\widehat h\circ\alpha$.

The abstract definition replaces these two set-valued Hom constructions by $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D}(F(-),-)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(-,U(-))$. An adjunction is a specified natural bijection between them.
If $\alpha$ swaps 0 and 1 and $\beta(n)=n+1$, either naturality route gives at $(0,a)$ the value $\beta(h(1,a))=8$. This is an explicit map-level check.
If $T$ intertwines all $g\in G$, it intertwines every $h\in H$. Identity maps and composites remain the same functions, so restriction preserves them.

passages.excerpt: \operatorname{Hom}_S(M\otimes_RV,W)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R\bigl(V,\operatorname{Hom}_S(M,W)\bigr)
Let $S,R$ be associative unital rings and ${}_SM_R$ a unital bimodule, so $(sm)r=s(mr)$. Let $V$ be a unital left $R$-module and $W$ a unital left $S$-module.
First verify the actions. The left $S$-action on $M\otimes_RV$ descends because $(sm)r\otimes v=sm\otimes rv$, using bimodule compatibility.
Let $T:M\otimes_RV\to W$ be $S$-linear. For fixed $v$, $\widehat T(v)(m)=T(m\otimes v)$ is additive in $m$ and satisfies $\widehat T(v)(sm)=T(sm\otimes v)=sT(m\otimes v)$.
For outer $R$-linearity, compute $\widehat T(rv)(m)=T(m\otimes rv)=T(mr\otimes v)=\widehat T(v)(mr)=(r\widehat T(v))(m)$. Equality at every $m$ proves $\widehat T(rv)=r\widehat T(v)$.
Conversely, let $f:V\to\operatorname{Hom}_S(M,W)$ be $R$-linear. The function $B(m,v)=f(v)(m)$ is additive in each variable.
The map $T_f$ is $S$-linear because $T_f(sm\otimes v)=f(v)(sm)=s f(v)(m)=sT_f(m\otimes v)$, and pure tensors generate the tensor product additively. Both inverse identities are explicit.

Addition is preserved by evaluation, so the outer correspondence is an isomorphism of abelian groups. If all data are modules over a common commutative ring $k$ with compatible central actions, multiplying $T$ by $c\in k$ gives $\widehat{cT}(v)(m)=c\widehat T(v)(m)$.
Under these identifications, tensor-Hom becomes the identity correspondence on $\operatorname{Hom}_A(V,W)$. This also checks the action when $A$ is noncommutative.
Tensor-Hom here says that maps $V/nV\to W$ correspond to maps $V\to W[n]$. A map from $V/nV$ has image killed by $n$, while a map into $W[n]$ kills $nV$, which proves the correspondence concretely.

For $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z$, the proposed rule $\overline a\otimes v\mapsto av$ in $\mathbb Z$ depends on the integer representative $a$. Moreover $\overline1\otimes2=\overline0\otimes1=0$ would be sent to two.

passages.excerpt: M\ddot u+Ku=0,\qquad Kf=\omega^2Mf,\qquad K_{ii}=k\sum_{j\ne i}n_{ij}n_{ij}^T,\quad K_{ij}=-kn_{ij}n_{ij}^T

Four identical point masses $m>0$ have equilibrium positions $r_1=a(1,1,1)$, $r_2=a(1,-1,-1)$, $r_3=a(-1,1,-1)$ and $r_4=a(-1,-1,1)$, where $a>0$. Every pair is joined by one massless central Hooke spring with stiffness $k>0$ and rest length $\ell_0=2\sqrt2a$.

Every equilibrium difference has two nonzero coordinates of magnitude $2a$, so every edge has length $2\sqrt2a$. For a nonzero vector $d$, differentiating the norm gives $\|d+v\|=\|d\|+(d/\|d\|)\cdot v+O(\|v\|^2)$.
Because the springs are unstressed, the extension has zero constant term. Squaring gives the quadratic potential $V_2=\frac{k}{2}\sum e_{ij}^2$, and $V_{\mathrm{exact}}=V_2+O(\|u\|^3)$ near zero.

The contribution of one edge to the force on mass $i$ is $-k n_{ij}n_{ij}^T(u_i-u_j)$, while the force on mass $j$ is its negative. Thus the diagonal stiffness blocks receive $k n_{ij}n_{ij}^T$ and the off-diagonal blocks receive $-k n_{ij}n_{ij}^T$.
Each term $\frac{k}{2}e_{ij}^2$ is nonnegative, so $K$ is positive semidefinite. The kinetic energy is exactly $\frac12\dot u^TM\dot u$ with $M=mI_{12}$.

For a translation $u_i=c$, every relative displacement is zero. For an infinitesimal rotation $u_i=\Omega r_i$ with $\Omega^T=-\Omega$, the extension is $n_{ij}\cdot\Omega d_{ij}=\ell_0^{-1}d_{ij}^T\Omega d_{ij}=0$.
This edge contributes $kq^2/4$ to the potential. Its linear force on mass 1 is $-k(q/\sqrt2)n_{12}=(0,-kq/2,-kq/2)$.

For $u_i=\varepsilon\Omega r_i$, skew symmetry gives every first-order extension zero. The straight displacement path generally changes lengths at second order, while an exact finite rotation $u_i=(R-I)r_i$ preserves lengths exactly.
Adding an anchored spring or fixing one mass changes the allowed displacement space or adds a potential. A common translation then need not have zero energy.

Use the same four vertices $r_i$ and write any displacement as $u_i=c+Ar_i$, where $c\in\mathbb R^3$ and $A\in M_3(\mathbb R)$. These are coordinates for arbitrary small displacement data, not an assumption that the body remains rigid or that deformation is globally affine away from the four masses.
The vertices satisfy $\sum_i r_i=0$ and $\sum_i r_ir_i^T=4a^2I$. If $u_i=c+Ar_i$, averaging gives $c=\frac14\sum_i u_i$.
For arbitrary $u_i$, define $c,A$ by those formulas. At vertex $r_j$, $Ar_j=(4a^2)^{-1}\sum_i u_i(r_i\cdot r_j)=\frac14(3u_j-\sum_{i\ne j}u_i)=u_j-c$.
Let $v_i=d+Br_i$. Expanding the mass pairing gives $m\sum_i(c+Ar_i)\cdot(d+Br_i)$.
Every $A$ has the unique decomposition $S=(A+A^T)/2$ and $\Omega=(A-A^T)/2$. The spaces have dimensions six and three.

For a symmetry $R$ with vertex permutation $p$, the transformed displacement satisfies $u^{\prime}_{p(i)}=R(c+Ar_i)=Rc+RAR^{-1}r_{p(i)}$. Uniqueness of affine coordinates gives $c^{\prime}=Rc$ and $A^{\prime}=RAR^{-1}$.
